node.label: Philippe Ariès
node.date_label: Histoire des populations françaises et de leurs attitudes devant la vie (1948) · L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960) · Centuries of Childhood: Robert Baldick translation (1962) · L’Homme devant la mort (1977)
node.description: A historian of family, childhood and attitudes toward death whose work made familiar social arrangements appear historically variable. The childhood argument concerns the historical recognition of childhood; it is not equivalent to claiming that earlier parents never loved their children. Linda Pollock’s criticism questions evidential representativeness and generalization. Jean-Claude Chamboredon’s obituary places Ariès’s studies in dialogue with sociological questions about institutions and modernity, while explaining their politically and professionally unusual setting.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Histoire des populations françaises et de leurs attitudes devant la vie depuis le XVIIIe siècle (1948); L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960); Centuries of Childhood, translated by Robert Baldick (1962); L’Homme devant la mort (1977).
node.scope_note: Ariès’s complete books are unread here. Existing Pollock primary-excerpt qualifications are retained and Chamboredon is named as the substantive reader. No absence-of-parental-affection claim. French originals and Baldick’s translation remain distinct. The death-day discrepancy is kept in life research rather than resolved by assumption.

incident_edges.relationship: Makes the historical concept of childhood a problem for family history, while prompting disputes over sources and generalization.
incident_edges.evidence_note: The formulation retains Pollock’s distinction between concept and affection and her source criticism (1983 excerpt pp. 1–10, especially 2 and 6–9). It neither endorses Ariès’s chronology nor reassigns later writers’ stronger claims to him.

incident_edges.relationship: Historicizes familiar family institutions and social attitudes, opening comparative questions between modernity and earlier arrangements.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Attributed to Jean-Claude Chamboredon, 1985 pp. 150–151, on the work’s sociological questions and the family/death studies. This is a named reader’s substantive assessment, not a claim that Ariès belonged to a single sociological school.

incident_edges.relationship: While accepting Le Goff’s medieval cultural turning point, Ariès argues that his focus on purgatory as a place understates enduring older beliefs in repose and waiting (1983).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 153–156. Ariès accepts the terminus ad quem and cultural significance. His diffusion discussion allows regional variation and revises his own earlier late dating; this is no blanket denial of Le Goff’s thesis. French book (1981) not independently read.

named_group_routes.relationship: Childhood and family as historical subjects
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The demography umbrella's strand on childhood evidence (Ariès; Pollock) and its household studies can be read alongside Canadian childhood and family history, which grew from social and family history (Parr, ed., 1982; Bradbury, ed., 1992) more than from family reconstitution. PhD context: 12 of 132 PhDs engaging this group cite Ariès (9% vs 3%; lift 2.96). Comparison; no descent from Ariès is asserted.

verification.note: Publisher excerpt printed 1–10 read via OCR at https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/401759/9780521271332_excerpt_001.pdf ; pages 2 and 10 visually collated. Page 2 separates Ariès’s childhood concept from ill-treatment and later writers’ claims about parental formality. Pages 6–9 question generalization from public policy, a royal child and secondary accounts; page 10 records Stone’s fluctuating discipline alongside his claim of increasing concern. Excerpt ends during the literature review; Pollock’s own diary-analysis chapters and endnotes unread. Prior metadata retained in history. The separately checked 1981 thesis is not treated as identical to the 1983 book; Stone’s independently read 1979 abridgment has its own source record.

verification.note: Repository abstract and downloaded primary thesis read at pp. 31, 96–98 and 143–144. Supports explicit separation of Ariès’s childhood concept from affection, criticism of sweeping change/Stone’s explanatory wording and selective use of diaries, plus attention to literate diarists, censorship and generalization. Thesis and 1983 book are distinct records; no assumption of identical text. OCR dates in the repository abstract are unreliable and not repeated. Additional 2026-09-12 reading: complete section 2.2.3, printed pp. 93–94, criticizes deMause’s source selection and progressive narrative. Laslett/Shore quotations remain mediated; their predictions are not adopted. This is the 1981 thesis, not the independently unread 1983 book criticized by deMause in 1988.
